newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine wheat harvest proceeds in sunny weather.
newsitem.headline: Argentine wheat harvest proceeds in sunny weather.

text.p: Argentine farmers were in the fields Monday taking advantage of hot, dry weather to finish hauling in a bumper wheat crop now about 60 percent harvested.
The weather was benign not only for the wheat harvest, but also for the maize, soybean and sunflower crops, traders said.
Wheat output is heading for 15-15.5 million tonnes, according to different market estimates, despite storm damage earlier in the month in the heart of the southern wheat belt.

"The weather is now spectacular everywhere. It rained on the coast in the south on Saturday but since then it's been all sun," said one of the few traders to remain in baking Buenos Aires at what is the beginning of the beach season.
But while the harvest is now roaring along, the government estimates that about one million tonnes of output in the south was damaged by the storms and will have to be sold as fodder.
The wheat may have taken a battering, but the maize crop is enjoying this summer's steamy weather.
"Lots of rain, and now sun, it's very good for the maize," a trader said. He said that the market saw the government's estimate of production of 13.9 million tonnes as realistic.
This level of maize output would be up from 10.5 million tonnes in 1995/96. Wheat production last year was 9.2 million tonnes, according to the government.
Single crop soybeans are now beginning to flower in most areas, although the second crop is running a couple of weeks behind schedule due to delays in the wheat harvest.
Soil moisture for all crops outside of Cordoba province is good. Soybeans could do with regular rain, especially after reaching pod filling, but sunflowers prefer dry weather.

"In two weeks the sunflowers will be flowering all the way south. So they don't want heavy rains as that would wash the pollen away. Sunny weather would be ideal, especially as the soil moisture is at a nice level," a trader said.

While pointing out that some forecasts are for the weather to turn drier in January, he said he was estimating sunflower seed production from 5.0-5.2 million tonnes. He said that soybean production should total around 13 million tonnes given today's conditions.
Some sunflower plants were damaged by recent storms in the northern area of Santa Fe and in Chaco, which hit during flowering, but the loss in tonnage does not seem to be great.

The government estimates soybean output at 13.4 million tonnes, and sunflower production at 5.3 million tonnes. Argentina produced 12.4 million tonnes of soybeans in 1995/96, and 5.4 million tonnes of sunflower seed.
